## AI, in plain English

**AI** is the broad umbrella: technology that lets computers simulate capabilities such as learning, understanding, problem-solving, decision-making, creativity and autonomy. **Machine learning (ML)** is a part of AI in which an algorithm is trained on data to make predictions or decisions rather than being explicitly programmed for each task. **Deep learning** is a subset of ML built from multi-layer neural networks and is particularly useful for finding complicated patterns in large, often unstructured data. **Generative AI** is the deep-learning-based branch that produces new text, images, audio or video from a prompt rather than merely classifying or predicting. In supervised learning, one common ML approach, the training examples come with human-provided labels.

**Microsoft Copilot** is Microsoft’s AI companion for helping people create, brainstorm, learn and solve problems through chat across their day; its homepage also offers file upload, voice and cross-conversation memory when signed in.

A concrete workstation example is Intel’s newly reported **Xeon 600 “Granite Rapids-WS”** line versus AMD’s Threadripper family. Tom’s Hardware reports that Intel’s top Xeon 698X has **86 cores/172 threads**, a **2.0 GHz base** and **4.8 GHz boost** clock, **336 MB of L3 cache**, **eight memory channels**, up to **4 TB of memory**, and **128 PCIe 5.0 lanes**; it is rated at **350 W** base TDP. That puts its core count below AMD’s **96-core Threadripper Pro 9000 WX** flagship, although Intel says its platform’s 4 TB capacity is double the WX range’s and emphasizes expandability, AMX instructions and value. Intel’s own generational claims are up to **9%** more single-thread performance and **61%** more multi-thread performance than its prior workstation Xeons; importantly, Tom’s notes that Intel supplied **no direct Threadripper 9000 benchmarks**, so these are claims, not a demonstrated head-to-head win.

That hardware matters because demanding AI, rendering, engineering, scientific and data-analysis work needs lots of parallel CPU execution, fast/high-capacity memory for large datasets, and PCIe connectivity for accelerators and storage. Granite Rapids-WS also adds per-core AMX support with FP16 instructions; Intel attributes some of its AI-upscaling gains to those accelerators. In short: more cores help run more work at once, while memory bandwidth/capacity and accelerator connectivity help prevent big AI and professional workloads from waiting on data.

Sources used: [IBM’s AI overview](https://www.ibm.com/think/topics/artificial-intelligence), the [Microsoft Copilot homepage](https://copilot.microsoft.com/), and [Tom’s Hardware’s February 2, 2026 Xeon 600/Granite Rapids-WS report](https://www.tomshardware.com/pc-components/cpus/intel-returns-to-boxed-workstation-cpus-with-xeon-600-granite-rapids-ws-delivers-up-to-86-cores-4tb-of-memory-and-128-pcie-5-lanes). The requested Copilot homepage and Tom’s Hardware article have been left open for inspection.
